summary: Every IPv6 packet header carries a flow label field, yet in practice it is hardly used. This paper reviews what the standard says, covers the implementation issues, surveys published proposals for using the field, and finds most conflict with the standard. It also asks whether the standard should be revised.

plainLanguage.summary: Each IPv6 packet has a little blank name tag meant to say which conversation it belongs to, but nobody really fills it in. This paper looks at the ideas people had for using the tag and finds many break the rules.

questions: what is the ipv6 flow label
why doesnt ipv6 flow label get used
subtitle: What the IPv6 flow label field is for and why nobody uses it

tldr.problem: Every IPv6 packet has a 20-bit flow label field designed to identify packets belonging to the same flow, but it is almost never used in practice because the standard rules are very restrictive.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys various proposals for using the flow label to support quality of service, load balancing, and switching, and analyzes their compatibility with the flow label standard.
tldr.outcome: Most proposals break the standard rules, leaving the field effectively unused. The standard restricts encoding meaning in the label and forbids routers from assuming properties of the values, which limits practical applications.

today: RFC 3697 remains the current specification for the IPv6 flow label. The field is still almost universally set to zero in practice, and no comprehensive deployment of flow label usage has emerged. The tensions between the standard rules and practical deployment needs remain unresolved.

sections.title: The Flow Label Field and Its Purpose
sections.content:
The IPv6 flow label is a 20-bit field in every IPv6 packet header (bits 12 through 31) designed to mark packets belonging to the same flow so that they can receive the same treatment. The field is always present and never encrypted by IPsec, which makes it attractive for identifying traffic flows even when the transport-layer information is hidden. However, in practice today, the flow label is almost always set to zero, leaving 20 bits of each IPv6 header unused.

The flow label has a long history of debate within the IETF. Earlier proposals like CATNIP suggested using a label for fast switching in routers, while SIPP (which became IPv6) included it for requesting special handling like quality of service. The field survived several revisions, shrinking from 28 bits to 20 bits to make room for the traffic class field. Despite its inclusion in the standard, implementors largely ignored it, and today the flow label remains dormant in nearly every IPv6 packet.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 packets have a little number (like a ticket number) that says which conversation they belong to. Unlike other packet information, this number stays readable even when the packet is encrypted, which makes it useful for routers to treat related packets the same way. But the rules for using it are so strict that almost nobody uses it.

sections.title: How the Standard Defines the Flow Label
sections.content:
RFC 3697 standardizes the flow label with several key rules. The most important is that the 3-tuple of source address, destination address, and flow label value uniquely identifies which packets belong to a single flow. This avoids the "layer violation" problem: instead of needing to inspect port numbers in the transport layer (which may be hidden by encryption or fragmentation), a router needs only IP-layer information.

The standard also prohibits any encoding of meaning in the bit pattern. Routers MUST NOT assume any mathematical or other properties of the flow label values set by source nodes. This "dependency prohibition" is intended to prevent one host's encoding scheme from interfering with another's. The rule also states that router performance SHOULD NOT depend on the distribution of flow label values; the label bits alone make poor material for a hash key.

A final critical rule is that flow labels must be immutable: once a source sets the label, it must be delivered to the destination unchanged. Additionally, the same pair of source and destination addresses must not reuse the same flow label value within 120 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule says three things identify a flow: where it came from, where it's going, and this number. But the tricky rules are that nobody can peek at the bits to guess their meaning, and once set, the number can never change. These rules are supposed to keep different networks from breaking each other, but they make the field hard to use.

sections.title: Proposed Uses and the Compatibility Problem
sections.content:
Many researchers and engineers have proposed uses for the flow label to support quality of service, load balancing, and packet switching. Most proposals fall into a few categories.

Pseudo-random values: Some proposals suggest using the flow label as a pseudo-random identifier for fast lookups or to hash packets across multiple paths (load balancing). Others propose using it as a nonce to defend against off-path spoofing attacks on TCP.

QoS encoding: Several proposals encode QoS requirements directly in the flow label bits, using different bit patterns to signal delay, bandwidth, and packet-loss tolerances. Examples include directly parametric representation of QoS and extensions to the Diffserv model using the first few bits as codes.

Hop-by-hop switching: Proposals like IPv6 Label Switching Architecture (6LSA) treat the flow label like an MPLS label, changing it at each hop to signal local switching decisions. This directly contradicts the immutability rule and requires mechanisms like Diffserv code points to mark packets so routers know whether the label can be modified.

The problem is that almost all these proposals break at least one rule in RFC 3697. Even when designers try to respect the rules, they face fundamental limitations: the label can identify a flow but cannot convey information about QoS treatment or switching intentions.
sections.plainLanguage: People have many ideas: use it like a random ID for fast lookups, put QoS numbers in the bits, or have routers change it at each step like MPLS does. But each idea breaks the strict rules, like the rule that the number can never change. The strictness that was supposed to keep things compatible makes the field nearly useless.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Obstacles
sections.content:
Several practical obstacles prevent flow label deployment. First, there is no easy way for a router to determine whether a packet was sent by a host that is using a particular flow label scheme. Without knowing this, a router cannot safely decode the label according to its own encoding scheme without risking misinterpretation.

Second, open questions remain unanswered: what should a router do when it receives a packet with an unknown flow label? How long should flow label state be kept before expiring? For what kinds of applications should the flow label be set? These ambiguities make implementation decisions difficult.

Third, the immutability rule appears to exclude MPLS-like or CATNIP-like uses optimized for high-speed switching, which was a historical motivation for the field. This bars certain performance optimizations that routers might otherwise achieve.

Finally, DNS name resolution, mobility extensions in IPv6, and routing protocols have all attempted to use the flow label at some point but found its restrictions too limiting. The ROLL working group explicitly chose not to use the flow label despite initial interest, and the MEXT working group defined new mobility options instead of relying on the label.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers don't know if a host is using the label the same way they are, so they can't safely guess what the number means. The rules also leave real questions unanswered, like when to forget an old flow label or whether to change it at each hop. Even working groups that wanted to use it gave up and invented other mechanisms.

sections.title: The Standards Dilemma
sections.content:
The core tension is that RFC 3697's restrictions serve important principles. The immutability rule respects the stateless nature of the Internet and the end-to-end principle: the label belongs to the source, and no intermediate node should alter it. The dependency prohibition ensures that hosts and routers from different vendors or networks can coexist without unwanted interactions.

However, these design choices limit the label's practical utility. A protocol designer who wants to use the flow label to control switching or signal QoS directly must either accept these limitations or work within a restricted domain where all nodes follow a shared encoding scheme.

One approach to working around the restrictions within a domain is to have all internal hosts set the label to zero, let routers set and interpret the label internally according to their own rules, and have the last-hop router reset the label to zero before sending the packet beyond the domain. A hop-by-hop option could preserve the original flow label across the domain boundary.

Whether the RFC 3697 standard has sufficient value remains an open question. Given the numerous incompatible proposals, the failure of major working groups to use the field, and the absence of widespread deployment, it is reasonable to question whether the current rules should be revised to enable more practical uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The strict rules were meant to keep the internet from breaking when different vendors disagree on what the label means. But they're so strict that almost nobody can use the label for anything useful. Some people have ideas for working around the rules, but nobody is sure if it's worth the effort.
